newsitem.title: UK: U.S. debt to weather dollar/yen storm -analysts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. debt to weather dollar/yen storm -analysts.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries are likely to feel some pain from the recent slide in the dollar/yen exchange rate, but the downward impact is seen as limited, economists said on Thursday.
The plunge in dollar/yen in recent weeks prompted concerns in the U.S. Treasury market that the stronger yen could knock back recent hard-won gains and see investors backing out of the market.
But despite the sharp currency movement Treasuries have made modest gains.
"There's a negative bias (to Treasuries) because of the exchange rate movement," said Rob Hayward, economic adviser at BankAmerica in London.
"This has limited the upside on good news, but I would see the downside as reasonably limited as well."
The dollar has nosedived dramatically in the last few weeks, losing 12 yen or just less than 10 percent of its value since a 55-month high on May 1.
This has had big implications for investors who had taken advantage of a popular "carry" trade, where they borrowed in yen, exchanged the proceeds for dollars and then bought Treasuries.
They have profited from the yield pickup in the U.S. compared to the low cost of borrowing Japanese debt, but rapid currency moves can quickly turn lucrative trades into losses.
But so far the dollar's slide has not hit bonds too hard, economists said.
By 1308 GMT, June T-bond futures were down 14/32 at 109-23. The 10-year T-note/Bund gap was at 112 basis points compared to 111 at Wednesday's close.
"There is some edginess in the market, but looking at price performance the market has been holding quite well so far," Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International, said.

The resilience of Treasuries may be tied the perceived reduced chance of a U.S. interest rate rise at next week's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. Some analysts said the dollar/yen fall could still be take its toll.
"Given that the market failed to take advantage of fairly positive retail sales and other U.S. data earlier in the week it's bound to be a bit of a negative feature for the market," Hayward said.

But analysts said although the U.S. bond market was vulnerable to currency gyrations, dollar losses against the yen looked to have stabilised and reached a "comfort zone" for the near term which would also reduce its potential knock-on effect on bonds.

"On the currency side the market is trying to weigh up to what extent we could see a rapid move from these 115-type levels, because the authorities in Japan are making it pretty clear they don't want to see much more," Hannah said.
"It may be the market pauses a while at these levels which will dampen the effect on Treasuries for a time."
Economists said investors in Treasuries who were exposed to dollar/yen shifts would likely be defensive going into the May 20 FOMC meeting.
But they said investors exposed to carry trades were more likely to use currency hedging or switch out of yen to alternative sources of financing rather than offload Treasuries.
"Obviously leveraged investors will want to get rid of the dollar/yen part of their investment, " Adrian Schmidt, senior economist at Chase in London, said.
"This doesn't mean they are going to unload all their Treasury holdings, but they may want to hold somewhat less."
Schmidt said Treasuries could see some losses but added investors would primarily look to switch to financing outside the yen.
